directions: Anchor crowns in a nutrient-rich substrate under moderate to bright aquarium or pond lighting. The ribbon-like leaves spiral gently and the plant spreads quickly by runners, making it a workhorse background or midground species. Trim trailing foliage at the water surface to keep light reaching lower plants, and thin runners periodically to prevent overcrowding.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants

directions: This needle-leaved sedum forms a dense, trailing mat that glows chartreuse-gold in full sun and takes on orange and red tones in cold weather. It roots readily from broken stem pieces, so a few cuttings pressed into gritty soil will fill a bed or container within a season. Keep it out of soggy spots since standing water rots the shallow roots quickly.

Unlike the wide-running species form, this selection stays in tidy, non-invasive clumps topped with silver-mottled leaves and spikes of soft yellow spring flowers. It is a reliable filler for dry shade under trees where many groundcovers struggle. Cut back tattered foliage in late winter to refresh the clump before new growth emerges.

subcategory: tropical palm grown for heart and berry
directions: Native to Brazil's Atlantic Forest understory, this single-trunked palm produces small dark purple berries that are processed into a juice similar to acai. Young plants want filtered light and constant moisture, becoming more sun-tolerant as they mature over many years. Because wild harvest for its edible heart has made the species threatened, cultivated plantings are increasingly promoted as a sustainable source.

subcategory: Madagascar specimen tree with edible fruit
directions: This is the iconic, straight-trunked baobab of Madagascar's famous Avenue of the Baobabs, instantly recognizable by its bottle-shaped crown. Seedlings grow fast for the first few years in deep, free-draining soil before settling into the extremely slow, long-lived habit typical of the genus. Outside true tropical climates it is grown as a container specimen or bonsai-style tub plant, kept nearly dry through any cool dormant period.

Grown both as a cheerful starry yellow-flowered border perennial and for its fibrous corm, long used in southern African traditional medicine, this plant forms grassy clumps from a bulb-like base. It prefers a sunny spot with good drainage and resents being disturbed once established. Let the foliage die back naturally after flowering so the corm can store energy for the following season.

This gray-green, lobed-leaved poppy relative produces large brick-red to orange-scarlet blooms with a dark central blotch, followed by the long curved seed pods that give the genus its horned poppy name. It thrives in lean, gritty soil and poor-to-average fertility, flopping and flowering less in overly rich beds. Deadhead spent flowers to extend bloom, but leave a few pods to self-sow for next year.

A long-standing favorite in the planted aquarium hobby, this low, rounded-leaf creeper forms dense green carpets or mid-ground clumps under moderate to bright light. Grown emersed above the waterline, the same stems take on a more compact, paler form useful for paludariums. Pinch and replant tops periodically to keep the mat thick and prevent leggy, light-starved growth.

Known locally in South America as canafistula, this fast-growing legume tree produces airy, fern-like foliage and upright clusters of bright yellow flowers in summer. It is valued both as a durable timber species and as a shade or street tree in frost-free regions. Young trees benefit from staking in windy sites until the trunk thickens.

The type species of its genus, this Eastern Alps native forms a basal rosette of leathery, dark green leaves and sends up a dense spike of violet-blue, foxglove-like flowers in late spring. It is a staple of specialist alpine and rock garden collections, preferring cool summers and gritty, humus-rich soil that never dries out completely. Protect the crown from winter wet with a layer of grit or gravel mulch.

A fine-textured, semi-evergreen legume tree of the Sonoran Desert region, this species offers delicate, feathery foliage and a light canopy that makes it a popular low-water shade tree in Southwest landscapes. Clusters of small white puffball flowers appear in late spring, attracting pollinators. Established trees need little supplemental irrigation beyond occasional deep watering during extended drought.

This cane-forming terrestrial orchid sends up tall, leafy reed-like stems each growing season, topped with fragrant white flowers marked with an orange-fringed lip. After the canes mature and drop their leaves, water should be withheld almost entirely to mimic its natural dry season rest. Repot and divide clumps only while new growth is actively emerging for the best recovery.

A compact, spiny tropical shrub grown in dooryard fruit gardens for its small round fruit, whose soft pulp genuinely tastes like blackberry jam when fully ripe. Fragrant white tubular flowers appear through much of the warm season, followed by fruit that is best picked only once it softens and nearly collapses. It makes an attractive, easy-care hedge or container specimen in frost-free climates.

Bred at Canada's Morden Research Station as a non-seeding selection, this upright perennial produces narrow spikes of bright rose-pink flowers over a long summer season. Because it was developed specifically to reduce the seed-spread problems of wild purple loosestrife, it is a better-behaved border choice where legally available. Cut stems back hard after flowering to keep the clump tidy and encourage a possible rebloom.
sources: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, Morden Research Station

directions: A compact selection of the classic winged everlasting, this dwarf strain keeps the same papery white, button-centered flowers and silvery winged stems on a much shorter, more floriferous plant suited to borders and containers. It tolerates heat and poor soil well, flowering steadily from early summer until frost. Harvest stems for drying just as flowers open fully for the longest-lasting color.

This naturally shrubby form of the tree best known for the fragrance oil extracted from its flowers stays far smaller and more branching than the towering wild species, making it practical for home gardens and large pots. Its drooping, twisted yellow-green petals release a heavy, sweet scent most strongly in the evening. Give it rich, well-drained soil and shelter from strong wind, which can shred the flexible branches.

Small Bolwarra is a dwarf relative of the larger bolwarra (Eupomatia laurina), staying under a metre tall and spreading by suckers to form a low rainforest-floor colony. Its waxy, primitive cream-and-maroon flowers are pollinated by weevils rather than bees, a trait that reflects the genus's ancient lineage among flowering plants, and they ripen into small orange-red berries that birds and people both eat fresh. Give it permanent shade, leaf-littered soil, and steady moisture, since it is intolerant of sun exposure or drying out. It is slower growing and more cold-sensitive than its taller cousin, so is best suited to a protected courtyard or shaded understory planting.

Mexican calabash is a small, drought-hardy tree of Central American dry forests, instantly recognizable by its unusual cross-shaped, three-lobed 'donkey-ear' leaves clustered along the branches. Night-opening flowers are pollinated chiefly by bats and give way to smaller, harder-shelled globose fruit than true calabash, traditionally hollowed and dried into jicaro gourds for cups, maracas, and utensils. It tolerates poor, rocky, seasonally dry soils far better than Crescentia cujete and sheds its leaves briefly in the dry season. Site it away from foot traffic once fruiting begins, since the hard, heavy gourds can be a hazard when they drop.

Australian round lime is a rainforest citrus relative distinct from the finger lime, bearing smooth, round, yellow-green fruit rather than cylindrical ones, with a tangy pulp of small juice-filled vesicles similar in texture to finger lime caviar. The tree is self-fertile and does not need a separate pollinator plant. It is thorny and slow to begin fruiting from seed, so container-grown grafted trees are the practical choice for home gardens. Harvest when fruit colors fully and detaches with gentle pressure, generally in the cooler months.

Plum mango is a smaller-fruited relative of the Marian plum (Bouea macrophylla) already common in home orchards, producing clusters of tart-to-sweet, thin-skinned, plum-sized drupes with a mango-like resinous aroma. Trees bear perfect flowers and set fruit without a separate pollinator. Fruit is eaten fresh when fully ripe and soft, or pickled and used in sour relishes while still green, much as green mango is used in Southeast Asian cooking. It needs consistently warm, humid, frost-free conditions and is grown mainly in dooryard gardens across Malaysia, Indonesia, and Thailand.

The Panama tree is a huge, fast-growing lowland tropical shade tree with a distinctive flat, umbrella-shaped crown and a buttressed trunk at maturity. It bears both male and female flowers on the same tree, and the woody, star-shaped seed pods split open to reveal chestnut-like seeds that are edible raw or roasted once removed from the pod. Handle ripe pods with care, since the inner lining is covered in fine irritating bristles that embed in skin on contact. Because of its enormous eventual size, it needs a very open site and is best reserved for parks, large estates, or agroforestry plantings rather than small home gardens.
sources: Cayman Islands National Trust (Flora of the Cayman Islands)

directions: Lakshmi taru is a hardier, more compact relative of the Central American paradise tree (Simarouba amara), widely planted across India and parts of Central America as a fast-growing, drought-tolerant agroforestry species. Like other Simarouba, it is dioecious, meaning individual trees are either male or female, and only pollinated female trees produce the small olive-like fruit whose kernels are pressed for a high-yield oil used in biodiesel, soap, and cooking. It tolerates poorer, drier sites than S. amara and is valued for erosion control and quick canopy shade in degraded land restoration projects. Because sex cannot be determined until flowering, growers typically plant in groups to ensure both sexes are represented.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops & Plant Products

directions: The cow tree is a towering South American rainforest relative of the already-cultivated Maya nut (Brosimum alicastrum), famous since early 19th-century explorer accounts for the copious, sweet, nourishing white latex that flows from slashes cut into its bark and is drunk much like milk by rainforest communities in Colombia and Venezuela. It also bears small fig-like fruit typical of the mulberry family. This is an immense, slow-maturing specimen tree best suited to botanical collections or large tropical agroforestry plots rather than home gardens, and seed can be slow and uneven to germinate.

Macauba is a widespread tropical American relative of mbocaya (Acrocomia totai), ranging from Mexico through Brazil, and has drawn significant agricultural research interest as a New World alternative oil palm because a single fruit yields both a fibrous mesocarp oil and a separate kernel oil. The palm is monoecious, bearing both flower types on the same inflorescence, so a lone specimen can still set fruit. Established palms tolerate drought, poor soil, and occasional light frost better than true oil palm, but the densely spined trunk and leaf bases demand careful, permanent siting away from foot traffic. Fruiting does not begin for many years after planting.

Souari nut is an Amazonian rainforest relative of the already-cultivated pequi (Caryocar brasiliense), grown for its large, hard-shelled seeds enclosing rich, almond-flavored kernels that are eaten raw, roasted, or pressed for a fine cooking oil. Its showy flowers open at night and are pollinated chiefly by bats. Seedlings are exceptionally slow, often taking well over a decade to bear their first crop, so it suits long-horizon tropical plantings and botanical collections far more than typical home orchards. Give it deep, well-drained soil and room to eventually become a large forest emergent tree.

Dwarf sugar palm is a compact, suckering clumping palm from Taiwan and the Ryukyu Islands, grown almost entirely as a handsome landscape and container specimen rather than for sap or sugar production like its larger relative Arenga pinnata. Individual stems are monocarpic, flowering once and then dying back, but the clump as a whole persists and continues sending up new stems indefinitely. Its glossy, dark green, irregularly toothed leaflets and fuzzy black leaf-base fiber give strong textural contrast in shaded subtropical gardens. Handle ripe fruit with gloves, since the pulp contains irritating calcium oxalate crystals common throughout the genus.

Softcorkwood is an east-coast Australian relative of lemon aspen (Acronychia acidula), a smaller and notably more cold-tolerant rainforest-margin tree with distinctive soft, corky bark and fragrant small white flowers. The pale, translucent, tart berries that follow are used in native bushfood jams, cordials, and savory seasonings, much like other acronychia fruit. It tolerates a wider range of light and soil conditions than true deep-rainforest citrus relatives, making it a practical choice for native-garden plantings along the Australian east coast outside the tropics. Harvest fruit as it ripens from green to pale cream or pink.

This small evergreen tree, also called voavanga, produces round brown fruits with a tangy, tamarind-like pulp used fresh or in drinks and preserves. Plant in a warm, frost-free spot with deep, well-drained soil, watering regularly while young and tapering off once established. Trees tolerate heat and brief dry spells but grow and fruit best with consistent moisture and occasional feeding during the growing season. Fruit generally begins several years after planting on seedling trees, sooner on grafted stock.

Cang Zhu is a close relative of Bai Zhu grown for its aromatic rhizome, used in traditional Chinese medicine for digestive and damp-related complaints. It prefers humus-rich, well-drained soil in a lightly shaded woodland setting and resents waterlogging. Divide established clumps in spring or fall, and harvest roots after the plant has bulked up for at least two seasons. Keep beds weeded, as young plants are slow to establish and can be outcompeted.

Oval-leaf buchu is the larger-leaved counterpart to round-leaf buchu, long harvested from South African fynbos for its pungent, blackcurrant-tinged essential oil used in traditional remedies and flavoring. It thrives in lean, fast-draining, slightly acidic soil and needs excellent air circulation to avoid fungal troubles in humid climates. Water sparingly once established, since buchu is adapted to a dry-summer Mediterranean-type climate. Trim lightly after flowering to keep plants compact and productive.

This woody Amazonian vine is a traditional source of cat's claw, named for the hooked thorns it uses to climb, and is cultivated both as a curiosity and for its bark used in herbal preparations. Give it a sturdy trellis or host tree, rich organic soil, and consistent warmth and humidity year-round. It grows best in bright, filtered light rather than deep shade or harsh full sun. Protect from any chill, as it has no frost tolerance and sulks below the mid-50s.

Five-leaf aralia is a tough, arching shrub prized as an informal hedge or barrier planting thanks to its dense habit and sharp spines, with the variegated form grown for its cream-edged foliage. It adapts to poor soil, deep shade, and city pollution better than most flowering shrubs, making it a reliable choice for difficult sites. Prune after flowering or in late winter to control size and renew old wood from the base. Water regularly the first year, after which established plants tolerate considerable drought.

Baja Pitcher Sage is a fast-growing, heat-loving shrub covered in magenta tubular flowers that draw hummingbirds through much of the warm season. It wants full sun and sharp drainage, needing little supplemental water once roots are established. Cut back hard in late winter to keep the lanky growth tidy and encourage fresh flowering wood. It is a short-lived but vigorous plant, often self-sowing where conditions suit it.

Palm Grass is a clumping tropical foliage plant grown for its broad, pleated, palm-like leaves rather than for flowers, popular in shaded gardens and as a houseplant in cooler climates. It prefers filtered light to deep shade and consistently moist, humus-rich soil, resenting both drought and cold. Divide crowded clumps in spring to propagate and refresh vigor. Bring container specimens indoors well before frost in marginal zones.

The Be-Still Tree is a drought-tolerant flowering shrub named for its stiff, barely-swaying leaves, bearing small white blooms followed by clusters of fruit that ripen from green to black. It has a long history of traditional medicinal use and is also grown simply as an easy, tough landscape shrub in warm climates. Plant in full sun with well-drained soil and water only to establish, since mature plants handle heat and dry spells well. All parts contain latex and alkaloids, so site it away from areas where pets or children might chew on it.

Anacyclus depressus forms a flat, ground-hugging rosette of finely dissected, fern-like gray-green foliage that hugs scree and rock crevices. In late spring it produces solitary daisy-like flowers that open white above with crimson-red undersides and backs, closing at night and on cloudy days to reveal the red reverse. It demands exceptionally sharp drainage and resents winter wet far more than cold, so grow it in a raised bed, trough, or scree garden with plenty of grit worked into the soil. Established clumps are long-lived and spread slowly outward, making this a classic choice for alpine troughs and rock gardens.

Purple mint bush is a fast-growing, soft-foliaged Australian shrub prized for its profuse spring display of small tubular mauve-purple flowers that can smother the whole plant. The aromatic, mint-scented leaves are smaller and glossier than those of the related round-leaf mint bush, and the shrub quickly builds an upright, slightly open habit that benefits from a post-flowering trim to stay compact and floriferous the following season. It thrives in free-draining soil in full sun to light shade and is markedly drought tolerant once established, but like most Prostanthera species it is short-lived in heavy, poorly drained ground. Outside mild frost-free climates it is best grown as a container specimen protected over winter.

Senkyu is a clump-forming perennial in the carrot family grown in Japan and Korea for its aromatic rhizome, which is dried and used in traditional herbal preparations for circulation and women's health, often alongside dong quai. The finely cut, celery-like foliage and flat umbels of small white flowers resemble its carrot-family relatives, but it is the knobby, fragrant underground rhizome that is harvested, typically in the plant's second autumn once the tops have died back. Propagate by dividing rhizome sections rather than seed, since named stock is grown clonally in Japanese and Korean herb gardens. Give it consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, similar to the conditions favored by lovage and other moisture-loving umbellifers.
sources: Japan Kampo Medicines Manufacturers Association reference texts
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

directions: Mint shrub is a woody-based perennial subshrub from China grown for its narrow, serrated, strongly mint-scented foliage and its late-season spikes of small rose-pink to lilac flowers that appear in late summer and autumn when few other aromatic herbs are in bloom. It behaves more like a perennial than a true shrub in cold climates, dying back to the base each winter and resprouting vigorously from the crown in spring, so cutting the old stems down in early spring encourages the fullest flowering display. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established and is valued in borders both for its late nectar source for pollinators and for its crushed-leaf fragrance. Give it full sun and sharp drainage; it struggles in wet, heavy soils over winter.

Dorrigo pepper is a rainforest understory shrub native to the subtropical highlands of northern New South Wales, closely related to Tasmanian mountain pepper but adapted to warmer, subtropical rainforest conditions rather than cold alpine sites. Its glossy leaves and small berries carry the same peppery, warming heat associated with the genus, and both are used fresh or dried as a native Australian spice in bush-food cooking. It is dioecious, so a male plant must be grown nearby for female plants to set the fruiting berries used as a pepper substitute. Grow it in consistently moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in filtered shade, protected from hot drying wind and frost, and mulch heavily to keep the shallow root system cool and damp.
